claims.text: The FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are initially solid.
The tested FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles have a uniform size distribution.
In situ electron-microscope heating can track nanoparticle structural evolution at elevated temperatures.
The anticipated melting regime of these FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles is within approximately 600–1300 K.
Localized compositional segregation develops at the surface of heated FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Surface segregation triggers an initial liquid-like layer above a critical temperature.
Species with lower melting points preferentially segregate to the nanoparticle surface.
Surface segregation of lower-melting species increases local atomic mobility.
Increased mobility enables a transient liquid-like phase at the particle perimeter.
The premelting or melting front initiates at the particle periphery.
The liquid-like region propagates inward from the surface and culminates in complete melting.
The surface-segregation process governs both the onset and progression of the phase transition.
Liquid shells form at lower temperatures than would be expected for homogeneous bulk nucleation.
Similar-sized single-element nanoparticles show a narrower melting transition under identical heating conditions.
Similar-sized single-element nanoparticles have a higher and more uniform melting temperature than FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
FeNiCrCoCu particles larger than 20 nm may exhibit a different melting sequence or onset temperature.
High oxygen partial pressure may alter the melting sequence or onset temperature.
The surface-premelting temperature depends on particle size, composition, and local thermodynamic fluctuations.
Surface passivation can suppress compositional segregation.
Absence of surface-initiated melting or lack of correlation between a surface liquid-like layer and inward melting would falsify the proposed mechanism.
